rtr.x: HAVOC Watches are proud to be associated with the Royal Tank Regiment – one of the most historic and highly respected battalions in the British Army. With a legacy spanning more than a century, the Regiment has played a defining role in the development of armoured warfare and continues to represent the evolution of military capability. Their story is one of adaptation, professionalism and service shaped by generations of soldiers who have operated in some of the most demanding environments in warfare.

The Royal Tank Regiment is the oldest tank unit in the world – established in 1916 during the First World War as part of the Heavy Section of the Machine Gun Corps. It was formed in direct response to the deadlock of trench warfare, when early armoured vehicles were introduced as a new attempt to break static lines on the Western Front. What began as an experiment quickly proved its value and laid the foundations for what would become a permanent armoured force.

Since then, the Regiment has developed alongside the changing nature of armoured warfare. From the first improvised tanks of the Great War to the formidable world-class Challenger 2 tanks in service today, it has remained an operational armoured unit, adapting to shifts in technology, doctrine, and battlefield requirements.

At its core, the Regiment is defined by its people. Its history is marked by service in major conflicts across the globe, including the First and Second World Wars, campaigns in North Africa, and more recent operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. While the nature of warfare has changed dramatically over time, the standards expected of Royal Tank Regiment soldiers have remained constant. Courage, discipline and cohesion are central to its identity – forming the foundation on which operational effectiveness is built.

Alongside its operational functions, the Royal Tank Regiment maintains established traditions and commemorative practices that reflect its history and those who have served it. These customs sit alongside ongoing adaptation and modernisation, linking past and present while ensuring the Regiment continues to evolve to meet the requirements of contemporary military service.
The Battle of Cambrai

The Battle of Cambrai, fought in November–December 1917, marked a turning point in the First World War through the first large-scale, coordinated use of tanks in combat. While earlier deployments of tanks had been experimental and often mechanically unreliable, Cambrai demonstrated that armoured vehicles, when used in concentration and supported properly, could break entrenched defensive systems that had previously seemed impenetrable.

On 20 November 1917, British forces launched a surprise offensive against German positions near the town of Cambrai in northern France. Unlike previous offensives on the Western Front, there was no prolonged artillery bombardment beforehand. Instead, the British relied on secrecy and the shock effect of armour. Around 476 tanks were committed to the initial assault, supported by infantry and aircraft – the first time tanks were used en masse in a coordinated operational plan.

The initial breakthrough was striking. The tanks were able to crush barbed wire, cross trenches and suppress machine-gun positions, allowing British infantry to advance several miles in a matter of hours. This was a significant contrast to the stagnation that had defined much of the Western Front, where progress had been around 3 or 4 miles a year. The success at Cambrai demonstrated the potential of combining armour with artillery fire-for-effect, infantry movement, and air reconnaissance – an early example of what would later be recognised as combined arms warfare.

However, the breakthrough was not fully exploited. Logistical limitations, mechanical breakdowns, and exhaustion among advancing units slowed the British advance. Crucially, there was also a lack of effective reserves to hold captured ground. Within days, German forces regrouped and launched a determined counterattack and by early December, much of the ground gained in the initial assault had been recaptured, resulting in a strategically inconclusive outcome.

But despite the lack of a decisive territorial victory, by demonstrating what tanks could achieve under the right conditions, Cambrai marked a dramatic shift in British military strategy. For the first time, armoured warfare proved capable of delivering a rapid breakthrough against entrenched positions. The psychological impact was also considerable: German troops, previously confident in the invulnerability of trench systems, were forced to confront a new kind of battlefield threat.

The battle’s influence extended well beyond 1917 – British and German forces both began to adapt their tactics. The Germans accelerated development of anti-tank weapons and more flexible defensive systems, while the British refined armoured doctrine, emphasising coordination between tanks, infantry, artillery and air power. Although tanks at Cambrai were still mechanically fragile and tactically experimental, the lessons learned directly informed later operations in 1918, where armoured formations played a decisive role in breaking the stalemate of the Western Front.
While the First World War would not be decided by tanks alone, Cambrai ensured that armoured warfare would become a permanent and evolving feature of military doctrine in the decades that followed.

rtr.q: Accusing as I do without exception all the great Allied offensives of 1915, 1916, and 1917 as needless and wrongly conceived operations of infinite cost, I am bound to reply to the question, “What else could have been done?” And I answer it, pointing to the Battle of Cambrai: “This could have been done.”

rtr.x: From mud, through blood, to the green fields beyond.

The modern Royal Tank Regiment remains one of the most distinctive units in the British Army, from its origins in the Great War it has developed into a permanent armoured formation within the Royal Armoured Corps, providing the British Army’s specialist heavy armour capability.

At its core, the Regiment operates as Britain’s main tank unit. It is currently equipped with Challenger 2 main battle tanks, 62-tonne platforms armed with 120mm rifled guns and designed for protected firepower and cross-country mobility. Crews are trained to operate in high-intensity combat conditions as part of combined arms formations, where tanks work alongside infantry, artillery, engineers and reconnaissance elements. Training focuses on live firing on ranges such as Lulworth and Castlemartin, manoeuvre warfare, and operating within NATO command structures that require rapid integration with multinational units.

A Challenger 2 is crewed by four soldiers – commander, gunner, loader and driver – and effectiveness depends on coordination within the crew as well as between vehicles. Troops operate in squadrons made up of multiple tanks typically grouped into sabre squadrons and supported by HQ elements. The Regiment is structured to deploy at squadron or battle group level depending on tasking, with integration into larger armoured brigades when required.

Today’s RTR regularly participates in large-scale training exercises in the UK and Europe, including NATO exercises such as those conducted in Poland, Estonia and Germany. These exercises test interoperability between allied armoured and mechanised forces, including shared command systems such as the NATO communications architecture, logistics under deployed conditions, and the ability to operate in dispersed, multi-domain environments.
The Regiment also contributes to the British Army’s armoured readiness cycles, where squadrons rotate through high-readiness states for potential rapid deployment.

Alongside its tank squadrons, the Regiment includes reconnaissance and support elements that contribute to battlefield awareness and force protection. These capabilities include forward reconnaissance patrols, surveillance integration, and coordination with unmanned aerial systems used at brigade level. This supports armoured manoeuvres by providing intelligence on terrain, enemy positions, and movement corridors, allowing tanks to operate with greater tactical awareness and reduced exposure. While the image of the tank often dominates public perception, the reality is a far more nuanced system of capabilities working together.

Across the Regiment, training is continuous and highly structured. Crews rotate through driver training, gunnery qualifications, tactical exercises, and combined arms battle group training. Exercises often culminate in force-on-force scenarios at brigade level, where armoured units are tested in offensive and defensive operations under realistic battlefield conditions.

What makes the Royal Tank Regiment compelling today is their balance between permanence and change. The machines have evolved beyond recognition, the doctrine has been refined, and the operational environment has shifted repeatedly but the essential purpose remains – they are masters of mounted close combat, fusing mobility and firepower to shatter the will and cohesion of the foe.

The Royal Tank Regiment Association is comprised of serving and former officers and soldiers of the Royal Tank Regiment and its antecedent regiments. Membership is automatic upon leaving the Regiment, ensuring that no one who has served is ever disconnected from the wider RTR family.

The Association provides a lasting link between past and present, supporting welfare, remembrance, and regimental events while keeping the spirit and traditions of the Regiment alive long after active service has ended.

In partnership with the Association, HAVOC Watches are proud to offer the HAVOC 1917 – a timepiece which reflects our shared emphasis on precision, reliability and performance under pressure. Emblazoned with an iconic Challenger 2 tank and featuring the exclusive Regimental green, red and brown colours, representing their 1917 battlefield cry: from mud, through blood, to the green fields beyond.

scimitar-fearsome-scout.x: The CVR(T) Scimitar became a symbol of British armoured reconnaissance — a compact but formidable vehicle that served across deserts, mountains and some of the world’s most demanding battlefields.

To celebrate the legacy of this iconic machine, HAVOC Watches have created the HAVOC Scimitar – a precision timepiece inspired by decades of service, operational excellence and the enduring spirit of the soldiers who operated it.

Few British armoured vehicles have earned the affection and respect of soldiers quite like the CVR(T) Scimitar. Small enough to disappear into the landscape, fast enough to move ahead of armoured formations and armed with a powerful 30mm cannon, the Scimitar became one of the most successful reconnaissance vehicles of the modern British Army.

For more than 50 years, it served across some of the world’s most challenging environments. From the deserts of the Gulf War to the rugged terrain of Afghanistan, the Scimitar proved that a lightweight reconnaissance vehicle could still have a major impact on the battlefield.

The Scimitar’s story began with a simple military requirement: armies needed a vehicle that could see without being seen. While tanks provided the power needed to break through enemy positions, commanders also needed accurate information about what lay ahead. Where was the enemy? How strong were their defences? Which routes were safe for advancing forces?

These questions were answered by reconnaissance troops, the modern descendants of traditional cavalry scouts. Their role was not simply to fight, but to gather intelligence, identify threats and give commanders the advantage of knowledge.

The answer developed by Britain was the Combat Vehicle Reconnaissance (Tracked) family, known as CVR(T). Designed by British manufacturer Alvis, the family was created during the 1960s and focused on mobility, reliability and versatility. Rather than building large, heavily armoured vehicles, designers produced a series of compact tracked vehicles capable of operating across difficult terrain and supporting a wide range of battlefield roles.

The CVR(T) family included several famous vehicles, including the FV101 Scorpion light tank, FV103 Spartan armoured personnel carrier, FV104 Samaritan ambulance, and the FV107 Scimitar reconnaissance vehicle. Each used the same basic chassis design but was adapted for a different purpose.

The Scimitar entered British Army service in the early 1970s, following the successful development of the Scorpion. At first glance, the two vehicles looked almost identical, but their roles were very different. The Scorpion was designed as a light tank, armed with a 76mm gun, while the Scimitar was built specifically for reconnaissance and carried the impressive 30mm L21 RARDEN cannon.

That weapon gave the Scimitar a remarkable capability for a vehicle weighing less than eight tonnes. The RARDEN cannon could engage lightly armoured vehicles, enemy reconnaissance units and fortified positions, giving crews the ability to defend themselves if a scouting mission turned into a fight. It was supported by a coaxial 7.62mm machine gun and smoke grenade launchers, allowing the vehicle to manoeuvre and disengage when required.

The Scimitar’s greatest strength was its mobility. Powered by a compact engine and built on a tracked chassis, it could reach speeds of around 50mph while crossing terrain that would challenge heavier armoured vehicles. Its low profile made it difficult to detect, while its speed allowed crews to move quickly, gather information and relocate before attracting enemy attention.

Inside the vehicle, conditions were challenging. The crew consisted of three soldiers: a commander, gunner and driver. Space was extremely limited, and every crew member had to work efficiently. Reconnaissance required patience and concentration. A Scimitar crew might spend hours watching enemy activity before making a rapid movement to a new position.

This combination of observation and aggression made the Scimitar a perfect example of modern cavalry. It could move ahead of larger forces, identify enemy positions and, if necessary, strike with surprising force before disappearing again.

The vehicle’s first major combat test came during the Falklands War in 1982. British armoured reconnaissance vehicles, including Scimitars, played an important role during the campaign’s land operations. The difficult terrain of the Falklands was a challenging environment, but the Scimitar’s mobility allowed it to operate where heavier vehicles could not. Its reliability and firepower proved valuable during the advance towards Stanley.

The Scimitar gained even greater recognition during the 1991 Gulf War. Operating in the open desert environment of Iraq and Kuwait, the vehicle was ideally suited to a war of movement. British armoured reconnaissance units used Scimitars to screen advancing formations, locate enemy positions and support the rapid Allied advance.

One of the most remarkable aspects of the Gulf War was the way relatively small reconnaissance vehicles operated alongside much larger armoured forces. The Scimitar was not designed to fight enemy tanks, yet its accurate 30mm cannon gave crews a valuable capability against lighter armoured threats. In fast-moving desert battles, speed and information were often just as important as armour protection.

The Scimitar continued to prove itself after the Cold War ended. It served in the Balkans during peacekeeping operations, where its mobility and presence helped provide security in difficult environments. Later, during operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, the vehicle adapted once again to new challenges.

Afghanistan presented a very different battlefield from the wide-open deserts of the Gulf. Roads, villages and mountainous terrain created new threats, particularly from improvised explosive devices. To meet these challenges, upgraded versions of the CVR(T) family received improved armour, protection systems and other modifications to extend their service life.

The fact that a design from the 1970s remained useful decades later was a testament to the quality of the original concept. The Scimitar was never the heaviest or most technologically advanced armoured vehicle, but it possessed speed, agility and the ability to gather information in dangerous environments.

For generations of British armoured soldiers, the Scimitar became more than just a vehicle. Its distinctive shape, compact size and unmistakable engine noise made it instantly recognisable. It became a symbol of British reconnaissance — a vehicle built for crews who operated ahead of the main force and accepted the risks that came with seeing the battlefield first.

After more than half a century of service, the Scimitar was finally withdrawn from the British Army in 2023, ending one of the longest careers of any British armoured vehicle. Its replacement represents a new era of reconnaissance technology, but the principles that made the Scimitar successful remain unchanged.

The legacy of the CVR(T) Scimitar lies in its remarkable balance of speed, firepower and versatility. It was small, but it was never insignificant. It was lightly armoured, but it was never lightly regarded. Across deserts, mountains and training grounds around the world, the Scimitar proved that knowing where the enemy was could be just as important as defeating them.

For over five decades, the Scimitar carried Britain’s cavalry tradition into the modern age – a fast, fearless and highly capable machine that earned its place among the most respected armoured vehicles in British military history.

The CVR(T) Scimitar remains one of the most recognisable vehicles in Britain’s armoured history, earning a reputation for reliability, versatility and service across some of the world’s most challenging environments. sabre-hybrid-reconnaissance.x: The CVR(T) Sabre represented speed, precision and tactical awareness – qualities that defined generations of cavalry soldiers and their machines.

To celebrate the legacy of one of Britain’s most distinctive and remarkable armoured reconnaissance vehicles, HAVOC Watches have created the HAVOC Sabre – combining military heritage with contemporary craftsmanship.

For more than a century, cavalry has performed one of the most important tasks on the battlefield: finding the enemy before the enemy finds you. While the image of cavalry is often associated with horses and sabres, modern armies have continued this tradition through fast, mobile armoured reconnaissance vehicles.
One of the most distinctive British examples was the Combat Vehicle Reconnaissance (Tracked) Sabre.

Small, fast and surprisingly powerful, the Sabre represented the final evolution of Britain’s highly successful CVR(T) family. Designed for reconnaissance in some of the most demanding battlefield conditions, it combined excellent mobility with a potent 30mm cannon, giving crews the ability not only to observe the battlefield but to fight when required.

The Sabre was introduced into service in the early 1990s, in the final years of the Cold War and at the beginning of a period of major change in military operations. Its role was not to replace heavily armoured tanks, but to perform a different and equally important task: moving ahead of larger formations, identifying threats, gathering intelligence and allowing commanders to make informed decisions.
This was the traditional cavalry role for the modern age.

The Sabre belonged to the Combat Vehicle Reconnaissance (Tracked) family, developed by British manufacturer Alvis from the 1960s onwards. CVR(T)s were built around a simple but very effective principle: reconnaissance vehicles did not need to be the largest or most heavily protected vehicles on the battlefield. They needed to be fast, discreet and able to operate where heavier armour could not.

This approach produced one of Britain’s most successful armoured vehicle families. The CVR(T) series included the FV101 Scorpion light tank, the FV107 Scimitar reconnaissance vehicle, the FV103 Spartan armoured personnel carrier, the Sultan command vehicle and several specialist variants. Thousands of these vehicles were produced to serve British forces and overseas operators around the world.

The Sabre was created by combining proven elements of two existing vehicles. Engineers mounted the turret of the FV721 Fox armoured reconnaissance vehicle onto the hull of the FV101 Scorpion light tank, creating a compact tracked reconnaissance vehicle with improved firepower. The result was a machine that retained the excellent handling and mobility of the Scorpion while gaining the more capable weapon system of the Fox.

Its main armament was the 30mm RARDEN cannon, a weapon renowned for its accuracy and hitting power. Although the Sabre was much smaller than a main battle tank, the RARDEN gave it a serious punch against lightly armoured vehicles, enemy reconnaissance assets and defensive positions. It was supported by a 7.62mm machine gun, providing additional capability against infantry and close-range threats.

The Sabre’s greatest advantage was its combination of speed, size and firepower. Weighing approximately eight tonnes, it was light enough to cross terrain that would challenge heavier armoured vehicles. Its tracked suspension allowed it to move across mud, broken ground and difficult routes, while its compact profile made it harder for enemy forces to detect and engage.

For reconnaissance crews, this mobility was crucial. The Sabre could move quickly into forward positions, observe enemy activity, transmit information back to commanders and relocate before becoming exposed. In a fast-moving battle, the ability to see first could prove just as valuable as the ability to fire first.

Inside the vehicle, life was demanding. The three-person crew consisted of a commander, gunner and driver, working in a confined environment where teamwork and communication were essential. Reconnaissance soldiers needed confidence, patience and sharp judgement. They often operated ahead of the main force, where their observations could influence the decisions of entire formations.

The Sabre was not designed to fight enemy tanks in head-on engagements. Its strength was intelligence, speed and tactical flexibility. It could identify enemy movements, test positions, support larger armoured units and respond rapidly when situations changed. In this role, it represented the modern expression of a cavalry tradition that had existed for centuries.

During the Cold War, British reconnaissance forces trained extensively for a potential conflict in Europe. The threat of a major armoured confrontation between NATO and Warsaw Pact forces meant information gathering would have been vital. Units equipped with vehicles such as Sabre would be responsible for screening larger formations, monitoring enemy advances and providing early warning of attacks.

Although the large tank battles many expected never took place, the Sabre remained valuable during a period of changing military commitments. The end of the Cold War brought new challenges, with British forces increasingly involved in overseas operations, peacekeeping missions and rapid deployments. The need for mobile reconnaissance did not disappear; if anything, the ability to gather accurate battlefield information became even more important.

The Sabre was eventually withdrawn from British Army service in the early 2000s as newer technologies and vehicles began to reshape reconnaissance. Modern surveillance systems, improved communications and more advanced armoured platforms changed how armies gathered information, but the principles behind the Sabre remained unchanged.

Its legacy lies in what it represented: a highly mobile, adaptable armoured vehicle designed around the needs of the soldier. It was not built to dominate through size or brute force, but through speed, awareness and agility.

The CVR(T) Sabre was the final chapter in a remarkable family of British reconnaissance vehicles that served for decades. From the deserts of overseas deployments to the training areas of the Cold War, these compact tracked vehicles earned a reputation for reliability and effectiveness.

Fast, agile and armed with a weapon system capable of a powerful response when required, the Sabre was a fitting descendant of Britain’s cavalry tradition: move forward, find the enemy and provide the knowledge needed for victory.

The CVR(T) Sabre remains one of the most distinctive vehicles in Britain’s armoured history, and we are proud to honour its legacy with a premium timepiece inspired by its design, capability and service.

jtac.x: HAVOC Watches are thrilled to have created a timepiece inspired by Joint Terminal Attack Controllers – professionals who coordinate close air support in some of the most demanding fields of conflict.

JTACs are specialist operators who link air assets with troops on the ground, guiding aircraft onto targets during active operations. They work in fast-changing environments where timing and accuracy are critical, ensuring that aerial support is delivered effectively and safely in coordination with wider battlefield activity.

Joint Terminal Attack Controllers (JTACs) are responsible for directing aircraft in support of ground forces. Their role is to ensure that close air support is accurately delivered, authorised and fully coordinated with troops on the ground.

JTACs are embedded with frontline units including infantry, armoured regiments and special forces. From these positions, they communicate directly with aircraft such as fast jets and attack helicopters, identifying targets, confirming them under strict rules of engagement, and guiding pilots to the correct objective. They use secure radios and laser designators to mark targets and improve accuracy, particularly in situations where friendly forces are operating close to enemy positions.

A key part of the role is managing the use of airspace above the battlefield. JTACs coordinate aircraft movements alongside artillery fire and ground manoeuvres to ensure that all elements can operate in the same area safely and effectively, without conflict between different systems or risk to friendly forces.

In British service, JTACs are drawn from experienced soldiers and undergo a demanding qualification process. Training covers aircraft capabilities, weapons effects, targeting procedures, airspace control, and communications systems. Qualification is achieved through live close air support exercises, where candidates control real aircraft delivering live ordnance in controlled training environments.

JTACs played a significant role in operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, where close air support was frequently required in complex terrain and rapidly changing combat situations. Their ability to integrate air power directly into ground operations remains a key capability in modern British and NATO forces.
Today, JTACs are a critical component of Joint Fires Doctrine, ensuring that air power is applied effectively and safely across high-intensity environments.
Joint Fires Doctrine

Joint Fires Doctrine is the system used to plan and coordinate indirect and supporting firepower on the battlefield. It brings together artillery, mortars, close air support, attack helicopters, and other supporting weaponry so they are used together in a controlled coordinated way. This maximises combat effectiveness and, just as importantly, protects friendly forces.

Rather than treating each capability separately, Joint Fires Doctrine combines them to achieve a single tactical effect. For example, artillery may be used to suppress enemy positions, while aircraft strike hardened targets, and mortars provide immediate close support to advancing troops. These effects are planned together so they support each stage of the operation.

Coordination is managed through a network of support teams, JTACs and command elements who work from a shared operational picture. This ensures missions are properly authorised, accurately targeted, and timed to support ground movement.

A principal requirement of Joint Fires is airspace coordination. With aircraft, artillery trajectories, and unmanned systems often operating in the same area, strict control measures are used to prevent friendly fire incidents and ensure safe separation. These include defined control areas, targeting procedures and coordination lines used by all units involved.

In modern British Army and NATO operations, Joint Fires is fully integrated into combined arms warfare. It is planned alongside manoeuvres, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. This combines different capabilities in a way that produces a greater overall effect than any single system could achieve alone.
CLEARED HOT!

“Cleared hot” is the definitive, mandatory radio command issued by a JTAC which grants military aircraft clearance to engage a target. This critical phrase, emblazoned on the HAVOC JTAC watch, authorises a pilot to begin their attack run and deploy weapons. It is used under strict rules of engagement following a precise sequence of events:

jtac.q: THE 9 LINE BRIEF: The JTAC relays a standardised tactical briefing to aircrew with target coordinates, elevation, attack geometry and restrictions. READBACK: The pilot confirms the critical data to ensure total accuracy and situation awareness. FINAL AUTHORISATION: Once the JTAC ensures the attack aligns with the ground commanders intent and minimises collateral damage, they grant final release clearance with the “Cleared Hot” command.

jtac.x: During operations in Afghanistan, particularly in Helmand Province between the mid-2000s and early 2010s, JTACs played a critical role in coordinating close air support for British and coalition forces in some of the most heavily contested areas of the campaign. Fighting was often made up of small-unit engagements, ambushes, and complex attacks on patrol bases and checkpoints, where troops could come under sustained fire in difficult terrain and built-up compounds.

In areas such as Sangin and Musa Qala, British units regularly operated in close contact with insurgent forces, often with limited cover and stretched communications. In these conditions, JTACs were the link between troops on the ground and fast jets, attack helicopters, and surveillance aircraft overhead. When a patrol came under fire, JTACs identified enemy firing points, confirmed their position using maps, digital systems, and laser equipment, and directed air strikes to suppress or destroy those threats.

Speed and accuracy were critical. Air support often had to be brought in within minutes, sometimes while friendly forces were still under fire or moving to better positions. JTACs had to keep updating aircraft as the situation changed on the ground, making sure strikes were accurate and safe even when troops were close to enemy positions. Often, they controlled more than one aircraft at the same time, including fast jets and attack helicopters, while using surveillance feeds to keep track of what was happening.

These operations often took place in areas where insurgents used complex terrain, compounds, and irrigation networks to move between firing points and avoid detection. JTACs had to take into account civilian presence, strict rules of engagement, and fast-changing distances between friendly and enemy forces.

The effectiveness of JTACs in Afghanistan helped shape modern British and NATO close air support methods. Their ability to bring air power directly into small-unit combat allowed ground forces to stay in contact with the enemy while reducing exposure during prolonged firefights. It also reinforced the need for close coordination between air and ground elements in conflicts where enemy forces were mobile and used terrain for cover.

By the later stages of the campaign, JTACs were a standard part of deployed British formations, embedded directly within frontline units. Their work in Afghanistan remains a clear example of how close air support became a fully integrated part of modern ground operations, and how precise air control became a core battlefield capability.

In Afghanistan, close air support became a routine part of British operations, particularly during sustained fighting in Helmand Province where ground troops frequently engaged with insurgent forces. The scale and intensity of these engagements drove the need for tighter coordination between air and land elements, shaping how support was delivered in real time.

brough-superior.x: HAVOC Watches are delighted to announce our partnership with Brough Superior – legendary brand of ultra-luxury hand built motorcycles.

Favoured transport of Lawrence of Arabia, the Brough Superior SS80 is widely regarded as the Rolls Royce of motorbikes – we are honoured to offer a timepiece which pays homage to this legend of transport.

The Brough Superior SS80 was officially presented to the public in November 1922 at the British Olympia Motorcycle Show in London. The SS in its name stands for Super Sports, and the 80 represents George Brough’s ground-breaking guarantee that every bike could reach and sustain speeds of 80mph.

With only 1,086 SS80s ever hand-built, this icon of British transport is as rare as it was revolutionary. The SS80 stood out as one of the earliest expressions of what a high-performance motorcycle could be – setting a benchmark for refinement and speed in the early 1920s.

The SS80 combined meticulously selected components with precision assembly and tuning to deliver unusual consistency for its era. Its significance was not only its performance but the way it balanced speed with mechanical durability – offering sustained high-speeds without the fragility associated with early motorcycles. The SS80 was the first motorcycle tested to hold 80 mph reliably rather than just briefly achieve it. This emphasis on sustained performance mattered more than headline speed, because early engines and tyres were often stressed by heat, vibration and poor road surfaces over long distances.

This combination of reliability, engineering precision, and exceptional pace made the Brough Superior SS80 a reference point for performance motorcycling and helped establish a new expectation for what a premium machine could achieve.

In partnership with Brough Superior, HAVOC Watches are proud to offer the HAVOC SS80. Emblazoned with the iconic Brough Superior SS80 logo, this timepiece reflects our shared philosophies on precision, innovation and reliability under pressure.
The Brough Story

The Brough story begins in the early years of British motorcycle experimentation, when engineers were still working out what a high-performance machine should look like. The early 1900s William E Brough machines were relatively conventional for their time, but they established a crucial base of engineering knowledge: frame construction, engine integration and the pursuit of reliability at a time when mechanical failure was still common.

His son, George Brough, became the driving force behind what would later become the Brough Superior identity. A skilled rider and tester, he quickly developed a reputation for pushing machines beyond their intended limits and identifying weaknesses in design. Rather than accepting standard factory output, he focused on refinement – improving handling, finish and consistency.

In 1919 he founded Brough Superior, deliberately choosing the word “Superior” as a public statement of intent. It was not subtle branding; it was a challenge to every other motorcycle maker in Britain.

From the outset, the company adopted a radical low-volume, highly individualised production approach. Unlike manufacturers mass producing thousands of identical machines, Brough Superior motorcycles were built in very small numbers – even at peak production, often only a few hundred per year. Total output over the company’s original lifespan is estimated at 3,000-4,000 machines.

A key feature of the brand was its use of specialist components combined into bespoke assemblies. Engines were not typically manufactured in-house but sourced from respected engineering firms such as J.A. Prestwich Industries. These engines were then carefully selected, tuned, and integrated into Brough’s own chassis designs. This allowed the company to focus on precision assembly and performance tuning rather than full engine production.

Early models such as the SS80 and SS100 became defining machines for the brand. The SS80 was designed to reliably reach 80mph, while the SS100 aimed for 100mph – figures that were extraordinary for the early 1920s. At a time when many motorcycles struggled to exceed 50 mph consistently, these performance targets placed Brough Superior in a category of its own.

The finish quality also set the brand apart. Polishing, plating and detailing were carried out to exceptionally high standards, giving the motorcycles a reputation for both mechanical excellence and visual refinement. Buyers were not just purchasing transport; they were commissioning high-performance engineering tailored to exacting standards.

The combination of rarity, performance and craftsmanship quickly made Brough Superior machines highly desirable. Even decades later, surviving examples are among the most valuable vintage motorcycles in the world, with some models achieving auction prices well into six figures.

In essence, the origin of Brough Superior lies in a philosophy rather than a single invention: that motorcycles should not only be fast, but built with uncompromising precision, individuality and attention to detail.

brough-superior.q: A skittish motorbike with a touch of blood in it is better than all the riding animals on earth. It is the silkiest thing I have ever ridden.

brough-superior.x: Lawrence of Arabia: Brough Superior Superfan

T E Lawrence was one of the most recognisable figures of the Great War – mainly because of his role in the Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule between 1916 and 1918. A trained archaeologist, he was drawn into British military intelligence due to his knowledge of the Middle East, fluency in Arabic and understanding of tribal politics. Skills that would prove decisive in irregular warfare.

His reputation rested not on rank but on results achieved in extreme conditions. Working with limited resources and no conventional command structure, he helped coordinate Arab irregular forces in a campaign built on mobility, sabotage and disruption rather than set-piece battles. One of his most significant achievements was his involvement in the capture of Aqaba in 1917. Approached over an unforgiving desert route and struck from an unexpected direction, the operation overcame a position which was considered secure from land attack. The victory provided a vital supply point and strengthened the Arab strategic position.

He also played a central role in the sustained disruption of the Hejaz Railway, key desert supply line of the Ottoman Empire. Small, fast-moving raiding groups repeatedly targeted bridges, tracks and stations, forcing the diversion of substantial enemy manpower into repairs and protection. Though tactically modest in scale, these attacks had huge strategic impact by slowing movement and communication across the region.

By the end of the conflict, Lawrence had become both a practical asset and a symbolic figure. He received several British honours, including the Distinguished Service Order and appointment as a Companion of the Order of the Bath. He was also promoted within the military establishment, though his most significant contribution remained his leadership in unconventional operations rather than formal command. His role at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, arguing for Arab independence, further raised his profile, even if the political outcomes fell short of his aims.

After the war, he deliberately distanced himself from public life, enlisting under assumed names in the Royal Air Force and later the Royal Tank Regiment. He was deeply uneasy with the celebrity status that had formed around him and with the simplified myth of “Lawrence of Arabia” circulating in the press.

In his later life, he developed a powerful attachment to Brough Superior motorcycles. He owned at least seven machines, each tailored to his preferences, and used them as a form of escape from attention and obligation. They represented speed, control, and solitude – qualities sharply at odds with his public image.

During construction of his bikes he often specified adjustments to suit his preference for speed, precision and reliability over long distances. Their exceptional performance for the period made them ideal for his long, solitary rides. Their capacity for sustained high speed and mechanical dependability mattered as much to him as comfort or practicality. He valued the sense of control and isolation they provided, giving them pet names and describing them in deeply personal terms.

He said of one bike: “all this docile strength waits behind one tiny lever for the pleasure of my hand.” And of another: “Because Boa loves me, he gives me five more miles of speed than a stranger would get from him.”

This chapter ended in tragedy in 1935, when he suffered fatal injuries in a crash in Dorset after swerving to avoid two boys on bicycles while riding one of his Brough Superiors. He died days later, closing a life that had moved between desert warfare, diplomacy and retreat.
His legacy remains complex: a figure of extraordinary impact in irregular warfare and a man who spent his later years trying – never fully successfully – to separate himself from his legend.

The Brough Superior Club is the official organisation for the preservation and riding of vintage Brough machines. They support owners globally with a spares scheme, technical advice and regular get-togethers.

duke-of-lancasters-own-yeomanry.x: The Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry (DLOY) was one of Britain’s historic Yeomanry regiments, tracing its origins to the volunteer cavalry of Lancashire in 1798. Rooted in the communities of that county, it brought together generations of citizen soldiers who balanced civilian life with military service. Wearing the Red Rose of Lancaster as a symbol of their heritage, the regiment carried Lancashire’s name and traditions through more than two centuries of service.

From the battlefields of the Great War to campaigns of the Second World War, DLOY soldiers fought in some of the most demanding theatres of war, earning battle honours and a lasting reputation for courage, adaptability and commitment. Today, its legacy lives on through its successors, preserving the memory of the men who served under the Duke of Lancaster’s banner.
The Birth of a North West Cavalry Regiment

The DLOY came from a long tradition of British part-time cavalry, raised from local communities and shaped by the needs of the nation. Before tanks and armoured vehicles changed the battlefield, mounted troops were essential for reconnaissance and rapid movement. The Yeomanry existed to provide that capability – drawing its strength from the villages, towns and estates of the people it served.

The regiment that would become the DLOY began life during a period of growing concern about Britain’s military readiness. The late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries were unsettled years. Britain faced threats from revolutionary France, internal unrest and the possibility of invasion. The regular Army was too small to cover every requirement, so the government looked to local communities to provide additional defence. This led to the creation of volunteer mounted units across the country. These were not full-time soldiers. They were farmers, landowners, businessmen and professionals who trained in their spare time while maintaining their civilian lives. Many provided their own horses and equipment, and they were often led by local figures who had influence and standing in their communities.

The word “Yeomanry” reflects this connection – a yeoman was traditionally a freeholder or small landowner, someone who had a stake in the local area. Early Yeomanry units represented a partnership between the state and local society. They were built on the idea that communities could raise their own mounted defence forces when the country needed them.

One of the DLOY’s earliest ancestors was the Lancashire Yeomanry, raised in 1798 during the fears of a French invasion. Similar units appeared across the region as Britain prepared for the possibility of war with Napoleon’s France. These early formations were not intended to fight on distant battlefields – their main duties were closer to home. They protected important locations, supported local authorities during periods of unrest and acted as a mobile reserve. Their presence provided reassurance that communities were prepared and ready to defend themselves.

The defeat of Napoleon in 1815 reduced the immediate threat of invasion, and many Yeomanry units were downsized or disbanded. But the need for mounted volunteers continued – throughout the nineteenth century, new units were raised and existing ones reorganised as political tensions and military concerns changed.

The development of the Lancashire Yeomanry was closely linked to the industrial growth of the region. Lancashire was one of the world’s great manufacturing centres. Its mills, ports and towns were vital to Britain’s economy. A mounted force drawn from the area provided a valuable reserve that could respond quickly if needed.

The story of the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry begins with horses, local pride and a nation preparing for uncertain times. Its later achievements would be written on battlefields around the world, but its foundations were laid much closer to home, among the people who first answered the call to serve.
From Gentlemen Volunteers to Modern Soldiers

By the middle of the nineteenth century, the Yeomanry faced a challenge. The world that had created it was changing. The threat of invasion that had driven the first wave of mounted volunteers in the Napoleonic era had faded, while warfare itself was becoming more complex.
Rifles were improving, armies were becoming larger and the old ideas of the cavalryman charging across open ground was changing. If it was to remain relevant, the Yeomanry had to evolve.

During the Victorian era, the British Army underwent a series of major reforms designed to create a more efficient and professional force. Links between regular Army units and reserve forces were strengthened, training improved and a clearer structure for wartime mobilisation was developed.

For the Yeomanry, this meant a move away from wealthy local gentlemen simply gathering with their horses for occasional training. The traditional character remained – many officers still came from locals with long connections to their counties – but expectations increased. Troopers were required to train more regularly, follow military regulations and maintain higher standards of discipline.

Their role became more clearly defined – rather than being viewed as a force for dealing with local disturbances, they were increasingly seen as a valuable reserve of mounted soldiers. Their responsibilities included reconnaissance, communications, protecting supply routes and supporting regular cavalry formations.

Across Lancashire, Yeomanry units continued to reflect their communities. They provided a link between the Army and civilian society at a time when Britain’s global empire required military forces all across the world.
Yeomanry’s Greatest Test: the South Africa War

The South African War, fought between Britain and the Boer republics from 1899 to 1902, exposed serious weaknesses in Britain’s military preparations. The Boer forces were highly mobile mounted fighters who used the open terrain of South Africa to great effect. They avoided traditional set-piece battles and relied on speed, marksmanship and knowledge of the landscape.

Britain quickly discovered that it needed more mounted troops than the regular Army could provide – and so the Yeomanry became a vital source of reinforcements. Around 10,000 volunteers served overseas in the conflict, forming part of the Imperial Yeomanry created in 1900 specifically to serve in South Africa.

Yeomanry soldiers were no longer simply local defenders – they demonstrated that they could operate overseas in demanding conditions against experienced opponents. The campaign also highlighted areas where improvements were needed, including training, equipment and organisation.

The lessons of South Africa shaped the next major change in the history of the Yeomanry. In 1908, the creation of the Territorial Force brought Britain’s volunteer forces into a unified national reserve system. Yeomanry regiments became part of this new organisation, alongside volunteer infantry and artillery units.

This reform represented a new era. The Yeomanry kept its county identity, traditions and connections with local communities, but it now formed part of a planned military structure. Mobilisation arrangements were clearer, training became more consistent and the force was better prepared for the possibility of a major European war.

The transformation was remarkable. In little more than a century, the Yeomanry had moved from privately equipped local cavalry groups into a disciplined reserve force ready for modern conflict. The foundations were now in place for the challenges that awaited in the twentieth century – challenges that would test these soldiers on battlefields far beyond the counties where their regiments were born.
From Horsemen to Front Line Soldiers

When war was declared in August 1914, the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry was ready. The regiment had spent years preparing for the possibility of a major conflict but nobody could have predicted how quickly the nature of warfare would change. Within months, men who had trained as cavalrymen found themselves fighting in conditions far removed from the mounted warfare of their predecessors.

The DLOY mobilised as part of the Territorial Force and initially formed part of the Welsh Border Mounted Brigade. Like many Yeomanry regiments, its members were volunteers but the majority chose to accept overseas service when war came. The regiment was divided into separate elements, with different squadrons eventually serving in France, Egypt and Palestine.
This separation created a unique wartime story. Instead of one regiment following a single path, the DLOY contributed soldiers across several campaigns.

The first major commitment came on the Western Front. Headquarters and elements of the regiment moved to France in 1915, initially serving as cavalry. However, the battlefield had changed dramatically – the trenches of France and Flanders were inaccessible to cavalry. Barbed wire, machine guns and artillery made traditional mounted charges almost impossible.

The DLOY became part of III Corps Cavalry Regiment in 1916, alongside other Yeomanry units where they carried out reconnaissance, maintained communications and provided mobile support. These were men trained to move quickly, and those skills were invaluable even when horses were no longer central to warfare.

In September 1917, the regiment’s Western Front elements became the 12th (Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry) Battalion, Manchester Regiment. This was not a reduction in status. It reflected the reality of modern war. The Army needed experienced soldiers who could reinforce infantry divisions, and the DLOY brought with it years of training, discipline and field experience.

The regiment’s greatest transformation came in 1917. As the need for mounted troops on the Western Front declined, many Yeomanry units were dismounted and converted into infantry formations. The men of the DLOY faced a remarkable change: soldiers who had joined as cavalrymen were retrained to fight on foot.

Meanwhile, another part of the regiment followed a very different path. ‘A’ Squadron served in Egypt and later Palestine, where cavalry remained highly effective. The desert environment allowed mounted troops to operate with a freedom impossible on the Western Front. Here, the traditions of the Yeomanry found their natural battlefield.

Serving with formations of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force, the squadron took part in the campaigns against the Ottoman Empire. The Palestine theatre saw some of the last great mounted operations in British military history, where speed, mobility and endurance once again became decisive.

The First World War therefore became a defining chapter in the history of the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry. The regiment entered the conflict as a traditional cavalry unit, carrying forward more than a century of mounted service. It emerged having proved something far more important – that its soldiers could adapt to whatever modern warfare demanded.

The men of the DLOY did not simply preserve an old cavalry tradition. They carried that tradition forward, whether serving in the saddle, behind the lines in France, or fighting as infantry alongside the famous Manchester Regiment. Their achievement was not only survival through one of history’s greatest conflicts, but the ability to change when the battlefield itself was transformed.

Lieutenant General Sir Harry Chauvel led the Desert Mounted Corps during the final Palestine campaign. His mounted forces achieved some of the last great cavalry victories of the war, with speed and mobility proving decisive at Beersheba and Megiddo.
Palestine: the Return of the Horse

The First World War forced the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry to adapt in ways few could have imagined. The regiment entered the conflict as a cavalry unit but on the Western Front, those traditions collided with the brutal reality of modern warfare. Trenches, barbed wire and machine guns had transformed the battlefield. The horse, once the symbol of mobility and power, had become increasingly vulnerable.
But thousands of miles away, in the deserts and open plains of the Middle East, the horse still had a vital role to play.

For the DLOY, the Palestine Campaign represented a remarkable return to the type of warfare for which Yeomanry had originally been created. In France they were forced to fight as infantry but mounted troops in Palestine were once again able to use speed, movement and endurance to shape the outcome of a campaign.

The DLOY’s involvement came as part of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (EEF), which was formed to defend Egypt and drive Ottoman forces out of Palestine. By 1917, the campaign was under the command of General Edmund Allenby, who understood the importance of combining infantry strength with mobile forces capable of exploiting breakthroughs.

The conditions were very different from the Western Front. Instead of muddy trenches and narrow front lines, troops faced vast distances, difficult terrain and extreme heat. Water supplies, navigation and the ability to move quickly over large areas was crucial. These were challenges that suited experienced mounted soldiers.

The turning point came on 31 October 1917, when the 4th Australian Light Horse Brigade was ordered to capture the town of Beersheba in Palestine. Their objective was to capture the town’s water supply – without water, the British mounted forces could not continue their advance.

Late in the day, with Ottoman defences still holding and daylight running out, the Australian troops launched a mounted assault. Armed mainly with rifles and bayonets, they rode directly towards Ottoman trenches and artillery positions. The charge succeeded because the defenders expected the Australians to dismount before attacking, as cavalry normally did at the time. Instead, the horsemen carried straight on, overrunning the positions and securing the wells.

In September 1918, the final offensive, the Battle of Megiddo, was one of the most successful operations of the war. British forces broke through Ottoman lines, and mounted troops moved rapidly behind the retreating enemy, capturing roads, supply centres and large numbers of prisoners. The speed of the advance was extraordinary, covering ground that would have taken infantry much longer to cross.

For the DLOY and other Yeomanry units involved, Palestine offered a striking contrast to their experience in France. On the Western Front, they had learned that traditional cavalry warfare had been overtaken by technology. Their horses had largely disappeared from the battlefield, replaced by rifles, machine guns and artillery. In Palestine, those same mounted skills became valuable again. The ability to move quickly, scout ahead and strike at vulnerable positions helped deliver victory.
The campaign was more than just another chapter in the DLOY’s wartime service. It represented the final great expression of the mounted Yeomanry tradition.
World War II: from Cavalry to Gunners

When war was declared in September 1939, the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry once again answered the call – and once again adapted to the changing shape of warfare. Tanks, aircraft and motorised armies had transformed the battlefield and the DLOY adapted by becoming part of the Royal Artillery and forming two regiments: the 77th and 78th Medium Regiments, Royal Artillery.

It was a remarkable transition. The same qualities that had defined the Yeomanry for generations – mobility, discipline and the ability to operate over difficult ground – now found a new purpose behind the guns. The regiment was now delivering the concentrated firepower essential to twentieth-century warfare.

The 78th Medium Regiment saw active service in the Middle East, fighting in Palestine, Syria and Italy as part of 6 Army Group Royal Artillery. Here, the regiment operated in campaigns where artillery played a decisive role in breaking enemy positions and supporting advancing Allied forces. Its service in the Middle East placed the regiment in some of the most demanding theatres of the war, where terrain, climate and supply difficulties created constant challenges.

In Syria, Allied forces fought against the Vichy French in the Syria-Lebanon Campaign of 1941, securing the region and removing a potential Axis foothold in the eastern Mediterranean. Later, the regiment moved into the Italian campaign. The advance up the Italian peninsula was slow and costly, with German forces making full use of mountains, rivers and prepared defensive positions. Medium artillery helped overcome these obstacles by delivering sustained fire against enemy strongpoints, gun positions and communication routes.

The fighting in Italy was unlike the fast-moving campaigns elsewhere. Progress was often measured in yards rather than miles, with battles taking place around heavily defended locations such as the Gustav Line and later the Gothic Line. Artillery units were required to maintain accuracy while operating in difficult conditions, often moving guns along poor roads and through terrain that had been badly damaged by fighting. The work was demanding, but the effectiveness of Allied artillery proved essential in wearing down German resistance.

The 77th Medium Regiment followed a different path. After remaining in Britain and Northern Ireland during the early years of the war, it prepared for the Allied invasion of Europe. In June 1944, the regiment landed in Normandy shortly after D-Day and became part of the Allied advance across France and into north-west Europe.

The Normandy campaign placed enormous demands on artillery formations. The Allied armies had secured a foothold on the beaches, but breaking out of the Normandy bridgehead proved extremely difficult. German forces, particularly experienced armoured units, fought a determined defensive campaign around Caen, using villages, wooded areas and prepared positions to slow the British advance.

The DLOY supported operations during the Battle of the Odon, a crucial phase of the Normandy campaign where British forces fought to contain and weaken German armoured formations. The battle was part of the wider effort to draw German forces towards the British sector, preventing them from moving south against American forces attempting to break out from the beachhead.

Later, during the Battle of the Falaise Pocket, Allied armies closed the trap on German forces attempting to escape Normandy. This was one of the most decisive moments of the campaign. Thousands of German soldiers were captured, and large numbers of vehicles and equipment were destroyed or abandoned. Artillery played a vital role, providing the firepower needed to break resistance and maintain pressure on retreating enemy units as the German army attempted to withdraw eastwards.

The regiment also supported Operation Market Garden in September 1944, the ambitious Allied attempt to seize bridges across the Netherlands and open a route into Germany. The operation relied on speed and coordination between airborne troops, ground forces and artillery support. The DLOY’s guns contributed to the effort to maintain momentum during the advance, giving supporting fire as Allied formations tried to reach their objectives.

Although Operation Market Garden did not achieve all of its objectives, it demonstrated the importance of artillery in highly mobile operations. Guns had to be moved forward quickly, supplied continuously and positioned close enough to support rapidly changing situations. The campaign showed that artillery was no longer simply a supporting arm in the background; it was one of the decisive elements that allowed modern armies to advance.

The Second World War marked another decisive chapter in the DLOY’s long history. The regiment had begun life as mounted volunteers defending their local communities. It had fought as cavalry in South Africa and the Middle East, adapted to infantry warfare in the First World War, and now became a modern artillery formation supporting some of the largest operations of the twentieth century.

duke-of-lancasters-own-yeomanry.q: I said to the man who stood at the Gate of the Year: ‘Give me a light that I may tread safely into the unknown.’ And he replied, ‘Go out into the darkness and put your hand into the Hand of God. That shall be to you better than light and safer than a known way.’

duke-of-lancasters-own-yeomanry.x: The Iconic Uniform
Alongside an impressive battlefield record, the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry carried a proud visual identity reflecting its history as a county cavalry regiment.

The most recognisable feature of the DLOY’s ceremonial uniform was its striking scarlet tunic, worn with the traditional cavalry plume or feathered headdress. Such a uniform may appear a world away from the realities of twentieth-century warfare, but these distinctive features connected the regiment to the age when mounted soldiers were a visible part of public life.

The bright colours of Yeomanry uniforms served several purposes. In the nineteenth century, cavalry regiments placed great importance on appearance and tradition. Soldiers were expected to look impressive during parades, ceremonial duties and public occasions. The uniform reflected the confidence and pride of the local communities that supported these volunteer forces.
The DLOY’s ceremonial dress also reflected its Lancashire identity. Yeomanry regiments were closely linked to their counties, and their uniforms, badges and standards preserved those connections.

The feathered headdress was part of the wider cavalry tradition inherited from the British Army. Such features were common among mounted regiments and helped create a sense of distinction and continuity. Although they had little practical value on the modern battlefield, they carried symbolic importance, representing generations of service stretching back to the regiment’s formation.

The contrast between ceremonial dress and wartime equipment tells much of the DLOY’s story. The same regiment that appeared in scarlet tunics and traditional headgear on parade later fought in khaki during the Boer War, endured the trenches of the First World War, operated artillery in the Second World War and eventually became an armoured reconnaissance unit.

The uniform changed because warfare changed. The traditions remained because they represented the determination of successive generations to adapt while maintaining a connection with those who served before.
The Final Years and Enduring Legacy

The end of the Second World War brought another period of uncertainty for the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry. Like many Territorial Army units, the regiment had to find its place in a very different world. The immediate threat of a large-scale European war had disappeared, but the Cold War created a new requirement for trained reserve forces capable of reinforcing the British Army at short notice.

In 1947, the DLOY was reformed as an armoured regiment, equipped with modern vehicles which reflected the changing nature of reconnaissance on the battlefield. Crews operated armoured cars and other vehicles, gathering information, screening larger formations and providing commanders with a clearer picture of enemy activity.

The regiment kept close links to Lancashire, maintaining its recruiting base and local identity. Drill halls, annual camps and ceremonial occasions continued the connection between the regiment and the communities that had always supported it.

The post-war years, however, brought repeated changes to Britain’s reserve forces. Defence cuts and reorganisations reduced the number of Yeomanry regiments, with many historic units being amalgamated or reduced in size.

In 1967, further reductions to the Territorial Army brought another major change. The DLOY lost its status as a full regimental unit and was reduced to squadron strength, becoming part of a new reconnaissance formation within the Army Reserve.

Further changes followed during the late twentieth century. The regiment’s lineage continued through the Royal Mercian and Lancastrian Yeomanry, formed in 1992 when several historic Yeomanry units were merged. The new regiment brought together the heritage of units from Lancashire, Cheshire, Staffordshire, Derbyshire and Worcestershire, while preserving the identities of its predecessors through individual squadrons.

The DLOY name continued through B (Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry) Squadron, ensuring that the regiment’s history was not lost despite the disappearance of the original regimental structure. The squadron maintained its badges, traditions and ceremonial links.

The post-Cold War period saw Yeomanry soldiers once again deployed overseas. The Royal Mercian and Lancastrian Yeomanry and Queen’s Own Yeomanry provided personnel for operations in the Balkans, Iraq and Afghanistan, supporting regular forces in roles ranging from reconnaissance to specialist armoured and communications tasks.
In 2006, further restructuring placed DLOY traditions within the Queen’s Own Yeomanry, where B Squadron (Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry) continues to carry the regiment’s name.

From the volunteers who mounted guard against invasion in the eighteenth century, to the gunners who fought across Europe in the Second World War, and the reservists serving on operations in the modern era, the regiment’s history reflects over 200 years of citizens who repeatedly answered the call to serve.

As a proud member of the Duke of Lancaster’s Own Yeomanry, HAVOC founder Lee Johnson has designed a watch inspired by the regiment’s traditions, achievements and unmistakable identity. Created to complement the elegance of the DLOY’s ceremonial dress, the HAVOC Sentinel combines military heritage with timeless design.
